newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Cambodia considers Khmer Rouge peace demands.
newsitem.headline: Cambodia considers Khmer Rouge peace demands.

text.p: Cambodian peace negotiators said on Wednesday that the government, not the military, would decide whether to accept Khmer Rouge guerrilla demands for senior armed forces posts.

A working group of top armed forces officers and commanders of breakaway Khmer Rouge forces in northwest Cambodia met for the first time on Tuesday in the guerrilla stronghold of Pailin to discuss a merger of their forces and administration issues.

"It is not my duty to agree to the positions requested by the Khmer Rouge. It depends on the government," General Ke Kim Yan, armed forces chief of staff and head of the government negotiating team, told Reuters.

The guerrilla negotiators, led by divisional commanders Sok Peap and Ei Chien and including the son of dissident Khmer Rouge leader Ieng Sary, demanded one deputy chief of staff post, one regional military chief and three regional deputy chief posts.
They also want one deputy chief of staff post in the Interior Ministry and requested that the Pailin region remain under their control as a separate province from Battambang province, officials said.

The guerrillas are loyal to Ieng Sary, who was granted a royal pardon on Saturday from his role in the genocide perpetrated by the 1975-79 Khmer Rouge regime in which he was foreign minister and deputy premier.

"This is a big request from the Khmer Rouge side, so the government team on the working group cannot decide by itself. We only take their request to the government," said Em Mara, a Defence Ministry official and negotiator.
The official said the Khmer Rouge were not asking for immediate agreement from the government, but had said the administration should not delay its decision.
The breakaway commanders told the negotiators that some of their men still did not fully trust the government.

Sok Peap and Ei Chean, commanders respectively of the Phnom Malai and Pailin bases along the border with Thailand, broke from Khmer Rouge hardliners early last month and pledged loyalty to Ieng Sary and support for reconciliation with the government.

The two sides forged a ceasefire at landmark talks on September 5 in Thailand between Ieng Sary and co-Defence Ministers Tea Banh and Tea Chamrath, but Ieng Sary later said the government must clarify his legal status to ensure further progress.
The dissident leader was sentenced to death in absentia for his role in the genocide of more than one million people during the Khmer Rouge's radical Maoist rule.
King Norodom Sihanouk signed an amnesty on Saturday, allowing the working group to meet for the first time.
The Khmer Rouge signed a United Nations-brokered peace accord in 1991, but later reneged on the pact and fought the coalition government that emerged from elections in 1993.
